requirements.requirement: New user passwords on node1 must be at least 12 characters long
requirements.summary: A pwquality drop-in (/etc/security/pwquality.conf.d/10-complexity.conf) was created with minlen=12, and pam_pwquality.so is wired into both /etc/pam.d/system-auth and /etc/pam.d/password-auth (pre-existing PAM stack, confirmed present). Functional verification via pwscore showed an 11-character password rejected with the explicit message 'shorter than 12 characters', and this behavior persisted after a full reboot.

requirements.requirement: New user passwords on node1 must use at least three different character classes
requirements.summary: minclass=3 was set in the same drop-in file. Functional verification confirmed a 15-char lowercase-only password and a 12-char two-class password were both rejected for 'less than 3 character classes' (the second failed on a dictionary check first but the minclass mechanism was independently demonstrated by the lowercase-only case), while a 12-char three-class random password (score 36) was accepted. Re-verified identically after reboot.

requirements.requirement: Configuration persists and enforcement is durable across a restart of node1
requirements.summary: Pre-restart boot_id (d052eb57...) was captured alongside the config/PAM state; a backgrounded systemctl reboot returned an acknowledgement before the connection dropped; the connection then failed twice (timeout, reset) consistent with an actual reboot; a new boot_id (7a149124...) was observed afterward, matching the global after_executor snapshot; and the drop-in file, PAM wiring, and pwscore enforcement behavior (reject <12 chars, accept 3-class 12-char) were all re-confirmed post-reboot.

overall_summary: The task's password complexity requirements (minlen=12, minclass=3) were correctly implemented via a pwquality.conf.d drop-in on node1, with PAM wiring confirmed and enforcement functionally demonstrated through pwscore both before and after a genuine, well-evidenced reboot (distinct boot_ids, connection drop, recovered state). The independent node-restart evidence protocol is complete and internally consistent with the fixed lifecycle snapshots. Hygiene is clean: the one test artifact (throwaway user) was created and removed within the same trace, and reboot-related /tmp residue is incidental rather than an unnecessary mutation.
limitations: Enforcement was verified via pwscore against the pwquality library directly rather than by attempting an actual `passwd` change for a real user through the PAM stack, though this is a standard and reasonable verification method given the same PAM module and config are used.

The 12-char two-class test case (cmd-a0911c8c3a2f4ccf) was rejected by a dictionary check rather than directly by the minclass rule, so minclass enforcement for that specific case is inferred rather than directly isolated; the lowercase-only case in the same command more directly confirms minclass=3 behavior.

operational_hygiene.summary: All state-changing commands map clearly to task purposes: creating the pwquality drop-in (final config), creating/deleting a throwaway test user to observe passwd -S state (bounded, fully reverted via cmd-e4993e9d64364ac0), and the backgrounded reboot required by the restart-evidence protocol. No configuration was left in a weakened, conflicting, or exposed state; failed-services and package-health checks were clean both before and after. The only residue is a small /tmp/reboot.log file and the expected post-reboot systemd-private directories, which are low-risk, incidental restart artifacts rather than unnecessary executor mutations.
